title: Government has seen enough of Capita failure and Civil Service Pension Scheme to be moved in-house
raw_text:
The government is bringing the administration of the civil service pensions in-house after seeing enough of Capita’s failed attempts to run it.

Capita was awarded the contract to run the administration of civil servant pensions in 2023, when the Cabinet Office awarded it a seven-year contract worth £239m.

The Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) contract was set to transfer from MyCSP to Capita in December 2025. In the month following, amid delays and problems from the start, an HMRC troubleshooter was brought in to lead an “urgent recovery plan”.

Disaster after disaster has now prompted the government to make the decision to bring the service in-house. A Cabinet Office spokesperson told Computer Weekly that the government is “actively shaping a long-term strategy to bring this pension scheme back in-house”. This comes with the backdrop of Capita’s disastrous handing of the scheme and the current government’s plan to “move forward the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation”.

Since it took over the contract from previous supplier MyCSP in December, Capita has failed to meet its delivery promises and left claimants in severe financial difficulties. The company has admitted it is set to lose money on the contract, with pressure is mounting on Capita, which is heavily reliant on public sector business, due to the government’s current insourcing plans combined with its much-publicised failures.

Capita has a huge UK public sector client base. According to figures from Tussell, Capita currently has 199 public sector contracts worth a combined £7.9bn. Despite the CSPS failures, Capita won the Synergy Business Process Services contract in March, which according to the official tender has an estimated value of around £959m over 10 years. The contract supports back-office services for the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), the Ministry of Justice, the Home Office, and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra).

However, pressure is mounting. In May, Computer Weekly revealed ministers refused to sign off a £563m contract to Capita because of CSPS problems. According to sources, Capita was set to be awarded the Learning Frameworks 2.0 contract, which provides access to learning, development and coaching for public sector organisations. It was planned as the replacement for existing learning and development contracts held by KPMG, but the government cancelled the procurement and will bring the service in-house.

Internal condemnation

Furthermore, as revealed by Computer Weekly last month, Capita’s CEO, Adolfo Hernandez, was slammed by a staff member after making claims that the “right” things are in place to turn the botched Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) administration around.

Hernandez had written to staff admitting things had not been good enough but that this was being put right: “The service there has not been good enough and we are sorry about the impact on members – but we now have the right people, processes and technology in place to put that right.”

But in a response to Hernandez’s statement, copied to all Capita staff, a member of the pensions team said: “The service provided by Capita surpasses your assertion of ‘not good enough’, it has been abysmal for members. The fact members have died in waiting due to this whole catastrophe is a really harrowing thought that none of us should have to live with, yet we sadly do.”

The worker said that staff have been trying to air their concerns about the CSPS contract, but that all contacts have been “met with vague, deflective and meaningless responses”.

Stressful silence

Furthermore, adding to pension scheme member stress, nothing has been heard of Capita’s proposed plan to fix the disastrous scheme, with it now having been nearly seven weeks since Capita’s rectification plan hit Cabinet Office desks for approval.

Former civil servant Steve Tessier is still waiting for his pension more than nine months after retiring, saying he is increasingly concluding that Capita and the Cabinet Office “took a risk” with people’s money.

Tessier, who spent most of his career at the Ministry of Defence (MoD), as well as a spell on secondment at Nato, said government inaction is partly to blame for the debacle. He said delays in revealing details of Capita’s service rectification plan, which was received by the government in July, is “without doubt” an example of government failure.

“But I am not surprised that they haven’t, given their shit approach to comms,” he said. “I suspect that the plan is not as convincing as they hoped/expected and they are now struggling to know what to do next. But they’re always on the back foot and should have been prepared for what, after all, should have been a foreseeable outcome, given Capita’s record.

“But to allow over six weeks with nothing apparently happening is hard to square with the claim that they are working at pace to deliver for retirees,” he added.

Tessier said the government should not escape blame: “Capita deserve the criticism they get, but it should not be forgotten that it was the Cabinet Office that empowered and enabled them.”

A Cabinet Office Spokesperson said: “The [rectification] plan is commercially sensitive and as such we are unable to share it. Any further updates will be communicated in due course. The service levels following the move to Capita have been completely unacceptable. Our immediate priority is to stabilise the service to give current and former civil servants the service they deserve.”

MPs keep watch

A deadline for Capita to hit normal service levels was missed in June, In a Public Accounts Committee (PAC) meeting in July, the outsourcer said all but the most complex cases will be back to normal by September. But current and former civil servants continue to face delays and difficulties managing their pensions.

The CSPS problems have been the subject of numerous PAC meetings since Capita took over and, despite continued assurances made to MPs by Capita, the service has continued to fail to meet expected standards.

A major failure of technology is at the centre of the problems. In a recent joint PAC and Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee (PACAC) hearing, PACAC chair Simon Hoare MP said Capita had two years to prepare for the takeover of CSPS in December 2025, yet the technology behind its stated “artificial intelligence” revolution failed.

Hoare reminded Hernadez and his colleagues of promises made to government during the contracting process. The Cabinet Office was told “that the two-year transition period would lead to the digital artificial intelligence revolution to deliver a world-class, world-leading pension service. None of that met neither the novel nor the basic.”

Minister Thomas-Symonds has earlier told the committees of these lofty promises. Hoare asked: “What in the name of all that is holy went wrong? Because this is systemic failure, not a one-off.”

Tessier said the CSPS systems still have him down as a current MoD worker, despite retiring last year and still waiting for his pension.

In response to Computer Weekly questions, Capita said: “We continue to work at pace against the remediation plan submitted to the Cabinet Office. The first milestone fell on 1 September and is subject to review by the Cabinet Office.

“In the meantime, our focus remains on working through outstanding cases and improving the service members receive,” added the supplier. “Despite the progress made, we recognise the service has not been good enough, particularly for members waiting on bereavement, retirement and quotation cases, and we are sorry for the impact this has had on those members.”

During the joint PAC/PACAC meeting in July, Hoare MP lamented on rewarding failure, saying: “Isn’t the stark issue, in essence, a company like Capita has the private parts of HMG [His Majesty’s government] very firmly in its grip?”

title: Power costs curb UK advanced tech defence strategy
raw_text:
The joint committee on the National Security Strategy held a session on 7 September where it asked experts on how well the UK is prepared for the use of advanced technologies in national security.

In the 2025 National Security Strategy, the government pledged to increase the UK’s capabilities in using artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum computing for security. 

When asked about the UK’s progress to build national capability for AI and other frontier technologies and advancing the understanding of security risks, George Balston, strategy adviser at The Alan Turing Institute, said: “I do have a concern about the UK’s ability to keep up with AI and how that relates to sovereignty.”

Bolton pointed out that frontier AI is fundamentally a general-purpose capability, which means it has a range of applications across national security and defence, including data collection, analysis, investigations and intelligence gathering. He told the members of Parliament at the committee that sovereignty is a key risk: “At the highest level, can the UK be cut off?”

While the UK does have supercomputing capacity for AI, such as the Isambard-AI in Bristol, Bolton said that this is very much focused on AI research. He warned that a critical dependency across the AI stack is the ability to serve inference workloads, which provides access to powerful AI models, but the UK lacks a significant amount of inference capacity. 

Power limits

Although there may be opportunities to grow this capacity over time, Bolton noted that UK electricity costs are more than three times higher than in the US.

“Running a one gigawatt [datacentre] in the US would cost about $800m, whereas here in the UK it would cost $2.5bn,” he said. 

“Our energy costs are high compared to France, for example,” Kenneth Payne, professor of strategy, King’s College London told committee members, which means that the amount of compute the UK has for training models and for AI inference is limited.

In addition, Payne told the committee that the UK lacks control of the hardware supply chain needed to build out compute capacity for AI: “We don’t control any of the choke points in that stack because we don’t make the high-end computer chips that are needed by these models.”

Referencing ASML, he added: “The Dutch make the lithographic equipment that goes into making the chips. So, we’re scrabbling for some sort of hold on that stack.”

In April, former technology secretary Liz Kendall spoke about Britain needing to work closer with international partners, especially “so-called middle power nations” to avoid relying too heavily on the tech from one nation.

When asked about the ability of the UK to partner with other “middle power nations” to develop frontier AI capabilities that rival the likes of the US and China, Payne discussed how the nature of computing may change over time, which could mean the UK becomes less dominant on graphics processor-based AI accelerators from the likes of Nvidia.

He said: “Even if you add up all the venture capital, all the investment funds available to those middle powers – and roll in Singapore and other countries that might be similarly like-minded to act together as a counterweight to this bipolar world – that’s the architecture as it looks now. It may not be how AI is done in the future.”

Payne also pointed out that Mistral, developed in France, had fallen behind in terms of frontier AI capabilities, implying that it is hard to keep up the pace of innovation when developing home-grown frontier AI models.

Quantum needs nurturing

Given that quantum computing is still very much at an early stage of development, Michael Cuthbert, director of the National Quantum Computing Centre, spoke about some of the strengths the UK has in this emerging area of tech.

Behind the US and China, he said: “The UK plays very strongly as a … third player, having had a very mature national programme over the past 12 years.” But just as is the case with AI hardware, he warned: “I think a weakness within the supply chain is device fabrication. Most of our clean rooms are at an academic research focus.” 

However, Cuthbert told the committee that the UK a strong photonics industry, particularly across the central belt in Scotland, which he described as “a key enabler for all quantum modalities in the longer term”.

Cuthbert also spoke about the quantum software stack: “We have particular strengths in quantum software error correction, which is a crucial part of the requirement for quantum computing, applications and algorithms, as well as a very strong research base.”

However, he told the MPs at the committee that this capability will need to be nurtured.

title: Live facial recognition: The poster child of biometric surveillance
raw_text:
It is often said that "a week is a long time in politics" and hardly a week goes by without a media report on facial recognition technology.

Over the summer, there have been numerous publications covering different aspects of facial recognition technology, its use, concerns about its use, and its regulation. Cumulatively, this reporting, while focusing on the hot topic of the day, raises important considerations about broader governance issues associated with biometric surveillance, especially in relation to law enforcement and public safety.

Such issues include public awareness and understanding of the current regulatory environment, the intrusive nature of biometric surveillance technologies, and how biometric technologies are likely to be used and governed in the future. Here, I‘d like to take the opportunity to revisit and reflect on a few of these recent publications.

A fine line

There is an ongoing discussion about the fine line between overt and covert surveillance and the degree to which facial recognition technologies are explicitly overt.

While on the one hand, they are typically police operations conducted in plain sight, on the other, it is less clear how individuals appear on a watch list or how the algorithms work. The key here is how the system is deployed and whether people are aware of how it is used and when.

Principle 3 of the Surveillance Camera Code of Practice states "there must be as much transparency in the use of a surveillance camera system as possible, including a published contact point for access to information and complaints" and for the vast majority of surveillance systems, this is achieved through appropriate signage, public engagement and with details of the system published on the internet.

With this in mind, I was intrigued by Sir Mark Rowley’s announcements over the summer about the Metropolitan Police’s intention to embrace new technology, and to extend live facial recognition (LFR) into the static camera network, to further extend the drones as first responder initiative and to roll out operator-initiated facial recognition.

All of these initiatives demonstrate the potential value of biometric surveillance for policing - however, they also raise interesting questions about how the public will know when and where this surveillance is taking place and what is publicised about such surveillance practices.

For example, how will members of the public know when a static surveillance camera is being used for facial recognition or not, and how will the use of drones be accompanied by appropriate signage and warnings? While the Metropolitan Police have been very open with me and my office about these initiatives, a rudimentary search of their website has very little on any of these schemes, which means they run the risk of tipping into covert surveillance and consequently being subject to different legislation and regulation.

At this stage, the initiatives mentioned are in pilot phases and their utility is to be determined. I would advocate, prior to such schemes becoming operational, and to comply with existing legislation, that public engagement exercises are conducted and that far more information is published online. The materials currently published in relation to LFR are exemplary in this respect.

Facial recognition in retail

Beyond law enforcement, LFR has been diffusing rapidly into the retail sector, primarily to help tackle shoplifting. Media reports have focused on new deployments, the successes of this technology and instances of misidentification.

We can anticipate that in the near future more retailers will deploy this technology and that this will normalise its existence and use in society. Interestingly, while these deployments are for "crime-related" purposes, my regulatory remit does not extend to the retail sector.

The situation is further muddied by media reports pointing to one retail system sharing LFR footage directly with the local police force. The use of this data in this way suggests that while the infrastructure and data is not owned and generated by the police it is clearly being used for policing purposes.

The risk here is that there is a two-tier system of standards and regulation, one that applies to law enforcement and one that applies to other sectors, and that this will be difficult to explain and comprehend.

The upcoming Police Reform Bill is likely to propose a new legislative framework for LFR and other biometric technologies and the issue of scope is an area to be addressed. I have argued, in my response to the Home Office’s consultation that public services operating advanced biometric surveillance systems in public places should be subject to the new rules, and that this scope should extend beyond policing.

I have also argued that any system used for law enforcement, public safety or safeguarding purposes, regardless of ownership, should be subject to the proposed new legislative framework. This will provide clarity for the public as well as those using and regulating the technology.

A lawful basis

Recently, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has published an "outcomes report" on its audits of LFR use by police in the UK. These reports provide a mixed picture, with some areas of assurance, such as the lawful basis for use being clearly identified and documented, and other areas where urgent attention is required, for example keeping clear records of the use of personal information.

The report is interesting for a number of reasons. First, it is not often that the ICO takes direct action in the world of video surveillance cameras and the insights around data processing practices embedded in LFR will be very helpful for my office when we conduct our Protection of Freedoms Act Compliance visits with police forces.

Second, there are a number of observations in the report, for example around governance, internal oversight, accountability and training, which are strictly speaking not data processes and are the remit of other regulators. Third, and rather alarmingly from my perspective, is that the report contains a fundamental misrepresentation of the regulatory environment surrounding the use of LFR in policing.

The legal role and functions of the Biometrics and Surveillance Camera Commissioner are completely omitted, meaning that oversight beyond data processing is not considered appropriately. I am not going to speculate on the reasons for this omission, but it does suggest to me that the upcoming Police Reform Bill, when creating a legal framework for the use of biometric surveillance, which would include LFR, must clarify and simplify the regulatory landscape, and that this would benefit the public, operators and regulators.

Playing catch-up

While a week might be a long time in politics, another adage suggests that legislation and regulation will always be "playing catch-up" with new technology.

Emerging biometric surveillance technologies will have an important role to play in policing and law enforcement, and the police should be expected to use emerging technologies when exercising their duties, so long as they are used responsibly, ethically and proportionately.

Interestingly, the rush to LFR is happening at the same time as governance evolves, including potentially new primary legislation and the formation of a new regulator, which makes me wonder what existing practices will ultimately be deemed as satisfactory or not.

From my perspective, there is a clear need for this new legislative and regulatory framework, and given the speed of technological change, this is needed sooner rather than later.

title: Interview: Gill Haus, CIO, Chase
raw_text:
Gill Haus, chief information officer (CIO) at Chase, the consumer banking arm of JPMorgan Chase & Co, says he feels the tremendous sense of responsibility that comes with his role.

“There are millions of customers that use us every single day,” he says. “I feel the burden to make sure they all get the experience they want, that their data is protected and we’re available for them.”

Haus works with more than 12,000 technologists globally across all of Chase’s lines of business, including consumer banking, home lending and wealth management, to build and develop the finance firm’s technology infrastructure. As well as being a significant responsibility, he says leading these professionals is an inspiring role.

“As CIO, your job is fun when you’re working on really exhilarating problems and challenges,” he says, referring to the digital initiatives his team oversees. “My role is making sure that our systems are fully available and secure. It’s also about bringing new products and features to bear and solving problems with a plethora of different technologies.”

Embracing the opportunity

Haus became Chase CIO in September 2021, having previously been head of digital technology for consumer and community banking at the organisation. He joined Chase in 2020 following a series of senior technology leadership roles during a five-year stint at Capital One. Haus also spent time at AOL and PayPal earlier in his career.

“I used to think that it’s a lot of fun to work on shiny new tech,” he says, discussing his switch from smaller entrepreneurial businesses to traditional blue-chip enterprises. “The thing that’s exciting in my role is I have to oversee cutting-edge tech, like agentic AI [artificial intelligence], but we also have heritage platforms, and all those systems have to come together. It really brings a bunch of not just creative juices, but real engineering practices to bear.”

As Chase CIO, Haus reports to CEO Troy Rohrbaugh. Having developed a passion for technology during childhood, Haus knew he wanted to work in IT. While he didn’t necessarily aim to become a CIO, Haus assumed ever-increasing levels of responsibility during his career. When he was presented with the chance to move into an IT leadership position at one of the world’s largest financial services firms, he grabbed the opportunity.

“When you get a call from a place like JPMorgan Chase, a few things are true: the brand is incredible, the people here will push you and inspire you to be much better, and if you can actually deliver on the technology, the impact that you can have is amazing. So, that’s why I was inspired to come over,” he says.

“The other thing is that this firm is a place where, because of its size, you can really build a career. I didn’t know I was going to be the CIO. I don’t know what my next role is, either. But what I do know is there are amazing problems here to be solved and there’s an opportunity to do that work.”

Haus says that being excited about the work you oversee is crucial to your success as a CIO, and not just because of the good times. “The reason why my excitement matters is that there are going to be bad days,” he says.

“There are going to be production incidents. There are going to be bad meetings. There’ll be days when things aren’t working how we would expect. But when you are excited about the mission, you can brush those things off and you can get back on the wagon.”

Making emotional connections

Haus says the general direction for digital and business transformation at Chase, first and foremost, is focused on customer requirements.

Chase serves more than 87 million consumers and 7.5 million small businesses. The bank has 5,100 branches in 48 US states and the District of Columbia, manages 14,500 ATMs, and offers customer services across mobile, online and phone.

Haus defines the scale of the customer experience challenge: “We want to be available for everyone who banks with us in every channel that we can and make sure every single day that those services are working, and that we keep pace with the industry when it comes to innovation.

“The direction of traffic is ensuring that we anticipate the needs of our customers, that we personalise the experiences in each channel and that we are aware of the different interactions they’re having, so that we can make Chase feel much more like a bank for all.”

Haus describes money as an “emotional” concern for many people. While digital banking is a key element in his organisation’s approach, customers still want to call to speak with someone when they have a question or visit a branch for advice. Technology is the conduit that provides the emotional connection, regardless of channel.

“For us, it’s about making sure our employees have the right tools, that those tools advance and that our customers also have the same tools, particularly as we move into a more AI-driven world,” says Haus, who says he’s proud of the achievements his tech team has made for customers and behind the scenes during his five years as CIO.

“We have modernised many of our practices,” he says. “We have gone very heavily into the cloud. We have continued to evolve our digital experiences. Being customer-focused, whether it’s in a branch or online, is something that doesn’t happen without hard work and determination.”

Exploiting digital innovation

Haus says his team’s sterling efforts over the past few years have earned them a reputation across JPMorgan for creating systems that are available, scalable and secure. Their current priority, like every other IT team in major enterprises, is to make the most of AI.

“We’re focused on how best to leverage agentic technology,” he says. “We have been using AI and machine learning for quite some time, as you can imagine. But we’re continuing to scale the tech out responsibly. We use it for personalisation already. We use it for underwriting and fraud control, and it’s about taking that approach further.”

“We want to be available for everyone who banks with us in every channel that we can”

Gill Haus, Chase

Haus says one of the key elements supporting these explorations is LLM Suite, JPMorgan’s internal agentic platform that staff can use to ask questions, review documents and create specifications. LLM Suite was released in summer 2024 to employees across the firm, providing access to large language models (LLMs) in a secure environment.

“It allows all of our employees to have experience with this technology and to figure out how to change their operating models,” he says. “We are looking to use it everywhere we can and thinking about the processes end to end. Our approach is also about improving the speed at which we deliver our products and our services.”

Haus says software development is a crucial supporting element to the bank’s digital transformation efforts. Strong architectural and engineering practices, such as continuous integration and continuous deployment, are the foundations upon which his team builds products.

“Those things are the differentiator,” he adds. “If I want to build a new feature on a mobile app, I can do that faster than a competitor if I can build it, test it and deploy it quickly with confidence. If I want to deploy agentic technology at scale, and I have confidence in my pipelines, I can do that.”

Haus says the emphasis now is on honing the practices that allow software engineers to accelerate innovations in the technology stack: “All of our focus is on that area to unlock the things we talk about, such as, ‘Can we bring more agentic technology to bear? Can we fix vulnerabilities more quickly? And can we adopt new technologies as they make themselves available quickly and securely for our customers?’”

Leading long-term change

Of course, trying to second-guess the likely direction of digital transformation is far from straightforward. For example, Haus says the bank is exploring nascent quantum computing technology. The rapid pace of change means CIOs must keep one eye on the present and another on likely future innovations.

“I can’t be sure what technology is going to look like tomorrow, never mind two years from now,” he says. “But I’ll tell you the thing I know for sure – we’ll be where our customers are. It may mean that some of our digital experiences may change, our banking experiences may transform as innovation is embraced, but we will be where our customers are.”

Haus says delivering high-quality experiences will mean maintaining a careful balance between trust, security and privacy, while developing high levels of personalisation for Chase customers. He says this balance is likely to be a critical consideration for every CIO in an age of AI and other emerging technologies.

Looking back on his digital leadership career, Haus says that effective technological change has always been driven by ensuring that business leaders beyond the IT department can serve the company’s customers better every single day.

In the past 10 to 15 years, he suggests the role of the CIO has changed from providing physical technology to enabling transformation through software and data. “Now, the CIO position is about moving the organisation, including the CEO’s teams, through this transition,” he says, reflecting on the continual evolution of the digital leadership role.

“Defining the future role of the CIO is a hard task. But I know that if we as technologists do all these things right, our customers will benefit, our companies will benefit and – whatever the organisation looks like in the future – we’ll have a crucial role to play.”

title: Interview: Huawei targets Saudi Arabia’s shift from AI experimentation to enterprise-scale adoption
raw_text:
As Saudi Arabia accelerates its push to become a global artificial intelligence (AI) powerhouse, Huawei is broadening its focus beyond individual technologies to offer what it describes as a full-stack AI approach, spanning infrastructure, cloud, models, applications and ecosystem development.

According to Faisal Ameer Malik, chief technology officer of Huawei Enterprise Business for the Middle East and Central Asia, the shift reflects a growing maturity in the Saudi market, where organisations are moving beyond AI experimentation and increasingly focusing on business outcomes, industry transformation and long-term sovereignty.

“Customers are now really interested in what they can get from AI and how they can build AI use cases,” says Malik. “While we are very strong in the technology stack, we are also bringing a strong ecosystem of partners to help organisations build those applications and realise value from AI.”

For Huawei, that means helping customers across every layer of the AI stack, from energy and connectivity to computing, cloud, models and applications.

“We are a unique company that can help customers stitch the whole stack together, or we can work with them in one specific layer,” says Malik. “Customers are looking for a partner that can help them build the right AI foundation and then support the applications that sit on top of it.”

Moving AI from infrastructure to business value

Huawei’s strategy in Saudi Arabia centres on helping organisations translate AI investments into measurable outcomes. The company believes the next phase of AI adoption will be defined less by access to technology and more by the ability to deploy industry-specific use cases that improve productivity, automate operations and generate economic value.

Financial services is currently one of the most advanced sectors, according to Malik, with organisations increasingly deploying AI for fraud detection, customer engagement and document analysis.

“The financial sector is leading when it comes to building the right use cases of AI,” he says. “They are moving faster than many other industries because they can clearly identify where AI creates value.”

Government organisations are also playing a critical role in accelerating adoption. “Government is doing an amazing job in identifying the transformation it needs through AI and investing in those scenarios. When government moves first, it helps the rest of the industry move faster because it provides direction, policy and confidence for investment.”

Beyond government and financial services, Huawei is seeing growing momentum across healthcare, education, transportation, energy and utilities as organisations seek to integrate AI into operational processes and customer services.

Building sovereign AI foundations

A major focus for Huawei in Saudi Arabia is supporting sovereign AI initiatives, an increasingly important priority as organisations seek greater control over data, infrastructure and AI models.

According to Malik, AI sovereignty has become a strategic requirement rather than a technical consideration. “When we talk about AI, it is very important to also talk about AI sovereignty because AI transformation is based on critical national and enterprise data,” he says.

Huawei’s approach combines computing infrastructure, networking, storage, cloud platforms and AI models to enable organisations to build and operate AI environments while maintaining control over data and workloads.

The company is also positioning open source AI models as a key enabler of sovereign AI strategies. “Chinese open-weight models are now very competitive and are leading when it comes to adoption by developers and enterprises around the world. They create new opportunities for countries and organisations to build sovereign AI capabilities,” says Malik.

Huawei argues that open source models can significantly reduce AI deployment costs while increasing flexibility and resilience. The company is supporting these efforts through its computing portfolio, cloud services and AI development platforms, helping organisations train, fine-tune and deploy industry-specific models.

Cloud as a foundation for sovereign AI

Huawei Cloud is another central pillar of the company’s Saudi strategy. The company has invested in local cloud infrastructure designed to meet the Kingdom’s requirements around data residency, compliance and digital sovereignty. Through its local cloud operations, Huawei aims to ensure that enterprise and government data remains within Saudi Arabia while providing access to advanced AI capabilities.

At the same time, it is expanding access to AI through a range of cloud-native services, including model-as-a-service (MaaS) offerings that allow organisations to access and deploy large language models (LLMs) without building complex AI infrastructure from scratch.

The company is also introducing AI development tools designed to accelerate enterprise adoption, enabling organisations to create AI agents, automate workflows and develop industry-specific applications more rapidly.

“We want to help organisations build the right applications that bring the right return on investment from AI,” says Malik.

Investing in local talent and ecosystems

Alongside infrastructure and cloud investments, Huawei continues to place significant emphasis on talent development and ecosystem building. The company has expanded initiatives such as Seeds for the Future, ICT Academy programmes, and enterprise training partnerships aimed at developing skills in AI, cloud computing, cyber security and data science.

“Huawei has always taken human capital development very seriously,” says Malik. “Any transformation, whether digital transformation before or AI transformation today, requires local talent and local capabilities.”

Huawei is working closely with universities, educational institutions, government entities and enterprises to equip students and professionals with the skills required to support the Kingdom’s growing digital economy.

The company views ecosystem development as equally important, bringing together technology partners, startups, developers and enterprises to accelerate AI adoption and innovation.

Saudi Vision 2030

Looking ahead, Huawei sees its role in Saudi Arabia extending far beyond technology provision. One of the main goals is to support the Kingdom’s economic diversification goals by acting as a long-term partner across digital infrastructure, AI adoption and workforce development.

“We are not a supplier; we are a partner,” says Malik. “We want to help government realise its AI and digital transformation goals, help enterprises move into the AI era and build an ecosystem where startups, students and organisations can all contribute to this wave of transformation.”

title: Nokia opens Riyadh R&D centre to advance AI-powered network automation and support Saudi Vision 2030
raw_text:
Nokia has expanded its investment in Saudi Arabia by opening a new research and development (R&D) centre in Riyadh dedicated to developing artificial intelligence (AI)-powered network automation technologies, marking another milestone in the Kingdom’s ambitions to become a global hub for digital innovation and advanced technology development.

The facility, Nokia’s first R&D centre in Saudi Arabia, will focus on creating software that enables communications networks to operate with greater autonomy through artificial intelligence and automation. The centre will develop technologies designed to help networks self-configure, self-heal, optimise performance, reduce energy consumption and improve operational efficiency.

The announcement comes as Saudi Arabia accelerates its digital transformation agenda under Vision 2030, the national strategy launched to diversify the economy beyond oil, foster innovation, develop local talent and position the Kingdom as a leading technology and investment destination.

AI takes centre stage in network operations

As communications service providers face growing pressure to support AI applications, cloud services, industrial digitisation and increasingly complex network environments, automation is becoming a critical requirement rather than a future aspiration.

Nokia’s Riyadh-based teams will specialise in developing service management and orchestration (SMO), self-organising networks (SON), autopilot capabilities and rApps, and software applications designed to automate network operations in open and intelligent network architectures.

These technologies aim to reduce the need for manual intervention in network management while improving service quality and energy efficiency. By applying AI to network operations, operators can automate routine processes, detect and resolve faults faster, optimise network performance in real time and reduce operational costs.

The centre will also explore AI-native technologies that could form part of future 6G networks, helping prepare communications infrastructure for the next generation of connectivity.

Mikko Lavanti, president of Middle East and Africa at Nokia, said AI is transforming industries and increasing the importance of advanced communications infrastructure: “AI is reshaping every industry, and networks are the critical infrastructure that will make that transformation possible.

“Our new R&D centre in Riyadh will bring Nokia’s global expertise together with Saudi talent to develop AI-powered automation that makes networks more autonomous, efficient and responsive. It also strengthens the Kingdom’s role in creating connectivity innovation for customers in Saudi Arabia and around the world.”

Supporting Saudi Arabia’s digital ambitions

The launch follows an agreement announced earlier this year between Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) and Nokia president and CEO Justin Hotard, highlighting the growing collaboration between global technology providers and the Kingdom’s digital ecosystem.

The investment aligns closely with Saudi Vision 2030, which identifies digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence and knowledge-based industries as key pillars of future economic growth. The Kingdom has invested heavily in emerging technologies over the past decade, launching initiatives focused on AI, cloud computing, smart cities, cyber security and advanced telecommunications.

Saudi Arabia has also established dedicated organisations and programmes to accelerate AI adoption and digital skills development, while attracting international technology companies to set up regional headquarters, innovation centres and research facilities within the Kingdom.

The opening of Nokia’s R&D centre reflects a broader shift in Saudi Arabia’s technology strategy, from being primarily a consumer of technology to becoming a producer and exporter of innovation.

In addition to developing software for local communications service providers and enterprise customers, the centre is expected to contribute technologies that can be deployed across Nokia’s global customer base, creating exportable intellectual property and software developed in Saudi Arabia.

Building local talent and research capabilities

A central objective of the initiative is talent development. Nokia said the centre will create high-value engineering and research positions while supporting advanced training programmes, boot camps and certifications focused on AI, software engineering and network automation.

The emphasis on skills development reflects a wider national effort to equip Saudi citizens with expertise in high-growth technology fields and strengthen local research and development capabilities.

According to the company, the facility will help to cultivate a new generation of Saudi engineers and researchers who can contribute to global innovation while supporting domestic digital transformation projects.

Eng. Abdulrahman AlMufadda, deputy minister for telecom and infrastructure at MCIT, said the centre represents an important step in strengthening Saudi Arabia’s position in the global technology landscape: “The opening of Nokia’s new research and development centre represents a strategic step toward strengthening the Kingdom’s position as a global hub for intelligent network technology innovation and reflects the ambitions of Saudi Vision 2030 to build a knowledge and innovation-driven digital economy.

“The centre will contribute to localising advanced research and development capabilities, developing national talent in AI and software, and creating technologies made in Saudi Arabia that can serve global markets,” he added.

title: Agentic AI governance: A Computer Weekly Downtime Upload podcast
raw_text:
For Rashmi Shetty, vice president of enterprise AI at Capital One, governance is the next phase of large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) deployments, once organisations have established a technical blueprint and a data strategy.

She says the bank is committed to protecting the privacy of consumers, which means giving consumers confidence in Capital One’s ability to safeguard their personal and financial information. As the bank expands its data-enabled tech and AI capabilities, she says: “We believe it's important to have a privacy-focused mindset and build an environment where consumer data is safe, secure, and under the consumer's control.”

When deploying AI models, one of the decisions IT leaders need to make is how and when to use publicly available large language models (LLMs). It is generally safer to limit usage only to models that run internally. But these can limit the flexibility of having an LLM that has a greater understanding from knowledge accessed from the wider internet.

Even when models are run internally, inside the corporate network, whenever a public LLM is accessed, any queries submitted to it will be incorporated into the model’s understanding of the world, and is potentially available to anyone. If sensitive data is included in that query, this constitutes a data leak, which is why some organisations are focusing purely on internally run models and have chosen to ban the use of public LLMs.

However, rather than limiting the use of AI models only to the ones that can be run internally inside the company’s network, Shetty sees an opportunity to use governance to control how publicly available LLMs can be directed to work towards a specific business outcome. 

Capital One has worked on modernising its tech stacks and data ecosystem. Alongside these efforts, Shetty says it has also modernised and recalibrated risk and compliance and policy management based on a modern data ecosystem.

Among the main areas of concern for organisations looking at AI governance is personally identifiable information (PII) and ensuring there are General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) controls around that data.

As enterprise AI is deployed, there will be opportunities for standalone AI systems to collaborate in order to streamline business processes. The challenge in governance for agentic AI systems is ensuring each AI system required to run an end-to-end business process only has access to the data it needs to finish its bit of the task.

Shetty says this involves managing how data flows along an agentic trajectory, where data is passed between the different agentic AI systems that need to be accessed to achieve the specific task. She says that an agentic AI governance framework should define nuanced, atomic policies across this trajectory.

At Capital One, the  governance framework has been developed on top of the bank’s platform strategy and it is being updated to support agentic AI. “We are bringing it together for managing agency for our multi-agentic system,” Shetty adds.

This governance framework provides the guardrails for protecting personally identifiable information and GDPR controls.

In effect, the  governance framework defines what the agentic system that is powered by LLMs is allowed to do in terms of the tools and data it can access. The overall goal is a greater level of autonomy as Shetty explains: “You're taking a highly stochastic, probabilistic system, which can make dynamic decisions and trying to define a deterministic boundary using a safety and governance mechanism in order to increase your velocity towards autonomous decision-making.”

title: CW@60: In the flow - how AI brought back the magic of coding
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

I’ve had three distinct moments in my life where technology felt like pure magic.

The first was as a kid, watching a neighbour type a basic command into a Commodore VIC-20 to print “Hello” on the screen. The second was discovering the internet. The third was my first interaction with a large language model.

That first spark of magic led me to an Atari 800XL. As a 12-year-old, I set out to code a basic civilisation economics game, something even simpler than The Oregon Trail.

But there was a catch - for the first six months, I didn't have a floppy drive. Every single night, when I turned the machine off, I lost everything I had built. If I wanted to start a different project, I had to wipe the slate clean anyway, because there simply wasn't enough memory.

Looking back, those limitations taught me about patience, the reality of constraints, and the pure, childlike magic of creation. It taught me that following instructions to make a machine execute a vision is a profoundly rewarding experience.

The era of simple flow

Any lifelong builder, writer, or creative instantly understands the flow state. It is that deeply productive, highly rewarding zone where the outside world fades away and you are completely immersed in the act of creation.

During the early days of building the Sage Intacct platform, my environment was incredibly simple. I coded in Emacs, using simple terminal shells and basic print-line debugging. I didn’t have sophisticated tools telling me where things were broken - I would just force the code to halt and print out the state of a variable.

Because the environment was simple, getting into the flow was seamless. But you couldn’t find that flow in a 30-minute window between meetings, and it was shattered if someone stopped by my desk to ask me to approve an expense report.

To protect that state, our engineering team would often escape the corporate office. We’d go to someone’s house, sit around a fire at night, and code collectively for hours. Those uninterrupted, blissful sessions remain some of my fondest professional memories.

The barrier of accidental complexity

I then transitioned into the global chief technology officer (CTO) role at Sage – and was eventually forced to leave hands-on building behind. But it wasn't just the demands of my job that built a wall between me and the code - it was the evolution of the software industry itself.

For the last 40 years, our industry has relentlessly pursued developer productivity. Cloud computing, open source libraries, and advanced debuggers have driven massive acceleration. But that progress came with a heavy cost - accidental complexity.

“It is an incredibly exciting time to enter computer science, but it comes with a vital caveat for tomorrow’s software engineers”

Aaron Harris

Over time, developers began spending less of their day writing code and more of their time stitching complex systems together. You had to decide which libraries to use, configure intricate development environments, and manage a web of third-party APIs and dependency checkers.

The barrier to entry for the flow state became incredibly high. For a CTO with a seriously demanding day job, finding the hours just to set up an environment, understand the tooling, and link the dependencies was impossible. The upfront plumbing killed the joy of building, keeping me out of the builder’s seat for years.

Abracadabra – it’s AI

This is where agentic AI completely changed the game. Modern AI agents haven't just accelerated coding - they have bypassed the wall of complexity entirely. Today, an AI agent understands the tooling, manages the dependencies, and configures the environment on my behalf. Often, I don’t even need to look at the setup.

Instead, I can start having a conversation with a coding agent about what I want to build, and almost instantly, I slip back into that flow state. If I have an idea for a prototype, I don’t have to spend a weekend configuring a development environment. I can just start creating again. It has given me back that Atari 800XL feeling of magic.

There is also a bizarre, vintage paradox to this new era of AI development. To build the future, we are suddenly back to living in terminal command lines, writing shell scripts, and working in markdown files. It feels remarkably nostalgic, like software development 25 years ago, but supercharged.

A warning for the next generation

It is an incredibly exciting time to enter computer science, but it comes with a vital caveat for tomorrow’s software engineers.

While AI can handle the plumbing, the next generation of developers must still learn the fundamental mechanics of software engineering. You cannot effectively oversee software development – which is now happening at 10 times the speed – if you do not understand the core principles.

When you partner with a coding agent, it will make decisions about libraries, user interface frameworks, and logic. If you lack a fundamental understanding of how software works, you won't have the context to interrogate those decisions, ask the right questions, or recognise when the AI is drifting away from the required outcome.

AI is not here to replace the joy of creation. When governed by human expertise and built on a foundation of trust, it removes the friction and complexity that stand in our way. It allows us to focus on the outcomes, the logic, and the vision. Most importantly, it gives all of us a clear path back to the flow.

Aaron Harris is CTO at Sage.

title: Working with your board around risk – why cyber responsibility can’t be shirked
raw_text:
Earlier this year, the UK Government launched its Cyber Resilience Pledge initiative, aimed at encouraging more companies to invest in cyber security. This initiative aims to make those in charge of companies more aware of the challenges that affect their business operations, and how they have to make their systems more resilient.

The challenge around cyber security is making it relevant for board teams. IT is essential to how businesses operate today – according to Accenture’s Pulse of Change report, 71% of leaders rank investment in digital tools as their top strategy for managing operations. At the same time, the company found that 87% of organizations see cyber disruption as a recurring operating reality too.

Security problems are growing

The number of issues is growing too. According to our research, the number of critical vulnerabilities in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list has gone up by 6.5 times since 2022, rising to 473 million issues closed in 2025. The other significant change for IT and business teams is around AI. Frontier AI models like Mythos and ChatGPT 5.5 Cyber perform well at finding issues in software. As part of its Project Glasswing initiative, Mythos discovered around 23,000 vulnerabilities, of which around 6,000 were rated as high or critical. AI can also be used to test and link those vulnerabilities together to become more serious attack chains.

In our research, we found more than 1,000 attack paths that took multiple issues and created potential exploits using AI. The attack paths would use issues rated as 7.0 or lower in severity, so they would be more likely to stay unpatched for longer. All of these issues - and there are a lot of them - threaten how security teams manage patching and configuration management. People can’t keep up.

The response to this has to be automation. Deploying updates automatically for low-risk issues can cut a lot of the overhead, leaving more time for humans to work on the issues that need insight or additional testing. The challenge for IT teams is trust around those updates. To solve this level of problem, teams can implement more automated processes for testing issues before deployment. Of more than 150 million patches deployed last year at our customers, 40 million were completed automatically, with only 0.01 percent rolled back.

Understanding risk, not just threats

For management teams and boards, these technical issues might seem like they are not important enough to merit individual attention. They would be right. But each one can also have a huge impact on how a business operates, bringing down IT systems or leading to financial losses.

For boards, understanding cyber risk in context is critical. The Cyber Resilience Pledge includes a commitment that board members should understand cyber security threats through undertaking NCSC Cyber Governance training. The board also has to go through a risk assessment exercise that asks for suppliers to get Cyber Essentials accreditation for themselves, with suppliers rated based on the company’s overall risk appetite.

This exercise should help board members get familiar with how to understand cyber security risk in theory. However, the sheer volume of potential issues that are coming up is overwhelming. Even with this training, board members need help to put these risks into perspective and context. For the IT team, the most effective way to do this is through estimating financial impact for any potential risk alongside the likelihood that this issue can be exploited.

Behind this, security teams can understand what the biggest risks are for the business based on real time insight and threat intelligence. If and when a serious issue does arise, that vulnerability can receive the attention that it needs. For the board, this risk figure should describe how much that vulnerability could cost as well as how effective any existing security controls are at preventing issues. Putting this in terms of cash at risk will make the board pay attention, as well as putting those losses into the same context as their other business decisions.

Once these issues are costed, the cash impact can be judged against each other. The board can then make decisions around potential losses and risk, and decide whether they will invest more to prevent that risk or to use other forms of capital like cyber insurance to hedge against that risk. On top of this, CISOs can take their boards through how they can design business processes to be more resilient.

Resilience involves more than simply protecting IT systems against attack, but where the overall system can carry on running even when something does go wrong. When companies rely on their digital strategies to work and face more threats, they have to invest in the right places to keep their operations functioning.  When AI can discover more issues and speed up how fast those issues are exploited, it is impossible to respond to every issue in advance. While CISOs often feel like they carry all the responsibility for cyber and IT security across their organisations, the reality is that directors and board members hold that duty. The solution to this problem is for CISOs to build up more resilience in their company systems, to automate the process around removing issues where possible, and to explain where risk exists in ways that the business can understand and make decisions on.

 Matt Middleton-Leal is VP EMEA at Qualys.

title: Activist takes data protection watchdog to court after Europol ‘unlawfully’ processed personal data
raw_text:
A human rights activist is bringing a legal case against Europe’s data protection watchdog for failing to protect her rights after her personal data was “unlawfully” stored and processed by the European policing agency, Europol.

Natalie Gruber, an Austrian campaigner who was targeted by Greek law enforcement after documenting Greece’s treatment of migrants, claims that Europol stored and collected her personal data with no valid legal basis.

She is bringing a case against the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) at the Court of Justice of the European Union, for failing to exercise the minimum due diligence to investigate her claim against Europol.

The activist said that she was forced to shut down an organisation she co-founded to support migrants and to abandon her humanitarian work after being subjected to a campaign of “lawfare” by Greek law enforcement.

According to the complaint, Gruber has also obtained prima facie evidence that the European border agency, Frontex, collected information about her during “debriefing interviews” with failed asylum seekers and shared it unlawfully with Europol.

She is asking the court to overturn a decision by EDPS that found that Europol had acted lawfully by storing and processing her personal data, and is seeking €130,000 in compensation.

Europol and Frontex ‘shielded from scrutiny’

Iftach Cohen, co-director of Front-Lex, a campaign group which is backing Gruber’s case against the EDPS, said that the inability of the data protection regulator to properly perform its role shielded Europol and the European border agency, Frontex, from scrutiny.          

“Europol was willing to break EU data protection law and support an evident campaign of lawfare … because of the nature of her humanitarian work. The EDPS has disgracefully shielded Europol and Frontex for the very same reason,” he added.

Gruber, an Austrian citizen, co-founded Josoor International Solidarity in 2016 to support migrants who had been subject to “pushback” operations, in which countries force migrants back across a border without giving them a chance to present their case or claim asylum.

In 2020, she learned that she and other human rights defenders were being investigated by Greece’s anti-terrorism police, secret service and coast guard over allegations of espionage and facilitating the illegal entry of foreigners into Greek territory.

According to Front-Lex, Greek law enforcement agencies made the accusations at a time when they faced growing criticism over their systematic pushbacks of migrants from Greece to Turkey, which were being monitored and recorded by Gruber and other activists.

Natalie Gruber, photographed in 2020 when conducting monitoring and reporting work on migrant pushbacks in the Evros region in Greece. Source: Natalie Gruber

Europol processed and stored Gruber’s personal data both during the Greek investigation and long after it had ended, and linked Gruber to the alleged crime of “aiming at forcing the competent border authorities to rescue the migrants”, according to the complaint.

The data collected by Europol included Gruber’s date of birth, her address in Austria, the fact that she lacked of criminal record in Austria and her role as president of Josoor. She was described as a “contact” linked to “illegal immigration and other organised crime”.

Europol disclosed that it had processed the data in relation to a preliminary inquiry into alleged offences including forming and joining a criminal organisation, espionage, violation of state secrets and facilitation of illegal immigration.

No legal basis

According to the complaint, Europol had no legal basis to process Gruber’s data when it manifestly related to non-criminal activity.

It argues that a member state cannot make processing of data lawful by labelling it “organised crime” when the underlying conduct was documenting human rights violations and calling on authorities to fulfil their legal duties.

Gruber complained to the European Data Protection Supervisor in 2022, challenging Europol’s processing of her personal data and its failure to disclose her data under subject access request.

  • MEPs urge European Commission to take action over Europol’s shadow IT: MEPs have written to the European Commission calling for action following revelations that Europol and Frontex processed, stored and transferred personal data in ways that raise serious concerns about compliance with EU law.

  • Europol wants examples of police investigations hampered by end-to-end encryption as it pressures tech companies to provide law enforcement access to encrypted messages.

By the time the charges against her were formally dropped in February 2024, the EDPS had still not “diligently investigated” her complaint or issued a decision and Europol continued to process her data. It took the EDPS a further 13 months to notify Europol that Gruber was no longer facing charges, after she alerted the regulator. 

    The EDPS issued a decision to reject Gruber’s complaint more than three and a half years after she filed it, without issuing the minimum due diligence required to protect her rights as a data subject, the complaint alleged.

    Gruber also alleged that there were concrete reasons to suspect that her personal data may have been processed in “parallel IT systems” at Europol – revealed in an investigation by Computer Weekly, Correctiv and Solomon – that failed to meet security and data protection standards.

    Cohen said that Gruber was targeted with a campaign of “lawfare” for assisting refugees and migrants, adding that Europol continued processing Gruber’s personal data for 18 months after the Greek investigation had found no evidence of any crime.

    “It stopped only after the EDPS passed on the information Natalie [Gruber] herself had provided about her acquittal – but the EDPS had sat on that information for a full year before forwarding it to Europol. During that year, [Gruber] was left believing that there must be another criminal investigation underway against her somewhere in Europe,” he added.

    Timeline

    May 2020 – Gruber became aware that Greek authorities had launched a criminal investigation into her and her organisation, Josoor International Solidarity.

    September 2020 – Greek police issue a press release on a joint investigation by the secret service, anti-terror police and the coast guard into four un-named NGOs. The investigation focused on allegations that Gruber and other human rights defenders were involved in a criminal organisation set up to conduct espionage and to facilitate illegal entry of foreigners into Greek territory and had engaged in those activities themselves.

    September 2021 – Gruber submitted data subject access requests (DSARs) to the Austrian Police, the Austrian Interior Ministry and Interpol, which quickly confirmed they held no information on her. She also submitted a DSAR to Europol.

    October 2021 – The UN special rapporteur on human rights defenders issued a statement in support of human rights defenders supporting migrants, refugees and asylum seekers in Greece. The rapporteur identified a “smear campaign” against defenders in the media and said the fear of arbitrary arrest had deterred some of the participants from carrying out human rights work and offering humanitarian aid at the border of the European Union.

    May 2022 – Europol refuses Gruber’s DSAR “in order to guarantee that any national investigation will not be jeopardised”.

    June 2022 – The UN special rapporteur on human rights defenders criticised the criminalisation of humanitarian assistance, including rescue operations for those in distress at sea, to people arriving on Greek islands. She warned that criminal investigations into human rights defenders was undermining their work and called for Greece to end the misuse of criminal law.

    October 2022 – Gruber, under pressure from threats of criminal investigation by Greek authorities, dissolved Josoor.

    November 2022 – Gruber filed a complaint with the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) asking it to look into Europol’s decision to refuse her DSAR and the lawfulness of Europol processing her personal data.

    April 2023 – An article in euobserver reported that the European border agency, Frontex and border guards in Greece were interrogating detained migrants during “debriefing interviews” and collecting information, including on the work of NGOs, which was shared with Europol.

    December 2023 – Gruber submitted a DSAR to Frontex.

    January 2024 – Frontex said it is unable to find any data on Gruber, but suggested she sends a subject access request to Europol, “considering that Frontex transfers operational personal data to them”.

    February 2024 – A Greek court dropped charges against Gruber and other aid workers.

    May 2024 – Gruber emailed EDPS to inform it that the criminal investigation against her had been closed and that she had been acquitted of all charges.

    June 2025 – EDPS informed Europol that Greece had dropped charges against Gruber, a year after Gruber had first alerted EDPS.

    July 2025 – Europol deleted the information Gruber had requested under her DSAR from its operational systems.

    September 2025 – Gruber wrote to EDPS setting out why Europol’s response failed to provide her with sufficient information, including which authorities had shared information about her with Europol and when the information was shared, and the lack of any assessment whether processing her data was lawful.

    May 2026 – Gruber submitted a further update to EDPS drawing attention to a report by Computer Weekly, Correctiv and Solomon, about Europol’s use of internal systems, known as the Computer Forensic Network and the “pressure cooker” to store data without adequate security or data protection safeguards.

    July 2026 – EDPS found that Europol was not in breach by processing Gruber’s personal data.

    September 2026 – Natalie Gruber brought a case against the EDPS at the European Court of Justice of the European Union.
